summary: Updates the ODETTE File Transfer Protocol, used for exchanging business data between trading partners, to version 2. It adds secure authenticated communication using TLS, file encryption, signing, and compression via CMS, and signed receipts. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ODETTE-FTP lets business applications exchange files and receive acknowledgments through an automated session. Version 2 adds security and compression options and updates the earlier specification.

questions: what is an eerp in oftp
subtitle: A peer-to-peer protocol for exchanging business files and acknowledgments.

tldr.problem: Business applications need to exchange files automatically between trading partners and receive acknowledgments when files arrive.
tldr.mechanism: ODETTE-FTP defines session and file-transfer commands, a virtual file representation, and optional session security, file security, compression, and signed responses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5024 is Informational, is not a candidate for an Internet Standard, and obsoletes RFC 2204. It was updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5024 is an Informational RFC published in November 2007. Its IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard; it obsoletes RFC 2204 and was updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Purpose and Virtual Files
sections.content:
ODETTE-FTP is designed for automatic file exchange between business applications. It provides a defined acknowledgment process for received files and is distinct from the interactive Internet FTP protocol.

Data is represented as a Virtual File so that systems can exchange files without depending on each other's local file format. The RFC defines record formats and ways to restart interrupted transfers; mapping a local file to the virtual representation is system-specific.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol moves business files between applications and provides a process for acknowledging their receipt. A Virtual File gives the protocol a common representation for systems with different local formats.

sections.title: Session and File Transfer
sections.content:
A session has phases for starting the session, starting a file, transferring data, ending the file, and ending the session. The peers take turns acting as Speaker and Listener, and commands indicate when a file begins, ends, or changes direction.

Data is sent in Exchange Buffers. Credit-based flow control limits how many buffers the Speaker may send before waiting for further credit from the Listener. The protocol also defines timers and error handling for session state.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers first establish a session, then announce and send files in buffers. The receiving peer grants credit so the sender knows when it may send more data.

sections.title: Commands and Framing
sections.content:
Each Exchange Buffer contains one command. Commands identify actions such as starting a session, starting a file, sending data, or ending a file. Session commands also carry negotiated details such as protocol level, buffer size, and transfer capabilities.

When ODETTE-FTP runs over TCP, a Stream Transmission Header gives the length of each buffer because TCP provides a byte stream rather than message boundaries. The RFC also specifies how data records are divided into subrecords.
sections.plainLanguage: Each buffer begins with a command that tells the receiver what the message does. Over TCP, a length header marks where that buffer ends.

sections.title: Receipts and Authentication
sections.content:
An End-to-End Response (EERP) acknowledges delivery of a Virtual File to its final destination. A Negative End Response (NERP) reports a non-temporary failure. A signed response can provide a signed acknowledgment when requested and supported.

ODETTE-FTP also describes authentication using a challenge exchanged between peers. The application is responsible for validating the result. Authentication does not decide whether a partner is authorized to exchange files.
sections.plainLanguage: An EERP reports successful delivery to the final destination, while a NERP reports certain failures. The application must still decide whether an authenticated partner is allowed to exchange files.

sections.title: Session and File Security
sections.content:
Session security layers ODETTE-FTP over TLS. File security can sign, compress, and encrypt a Virtual File using Cryptographic Message Syntax. File-level protection can remain with a file as it passes through intermediaries, while session security protects commands and data on a connection.

The RFC describes certificate use, algorithm choices, and security trade-offs. It notes that without security options, passwords are sent in clear text, and that authentication and authorization are separate decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS can protect an entire session, while file-level signing and encryption can protect an individual file. The RFC warns that passwords are exposed when security options are not used.
